newsitem.title: USA: Dollar up vs yen as US trade deficit less than feared.
newsitem.headline: Dollar up vs yen as US trade deficit less than feared.

text.p: The dollar jumped against the Japanese yen on Thursday following a government report that the April U.S. trade deficit, though up sharply from March, was smaller than expected.
But the dollar fell against the mark, as an indirect result of the German currency's strength vs. the weak yen.

Investors bought dollars, lifting the currency almost one yen after the Commerce Department reported that the trade gap in April was $8.36 billion, well below the $10 billion shortfall the market had expected but still up from a revised $7.76 billion in March.

The rise came despite an increase in the politically touchy deficit with Japan, which was expected to be a topic of discussion when the leaders of the Group of Seven industrial nations gather on Friday for a weekend summit in Denver.

"It seems to be a late burst of short-covering in front of this G7," said Bob Near, a vice president of corporate foreign exchange at Bank of New York, referring to dealers' buying back dollars after earlier sales on the belief the currency would fall.

"Maybe a lot of people were changing their minds," Near added. "We're not going to expect anything out of it that's going to put any heat on the Japanese surplus. That's what the markets seem to be telling us."
The dollar rose to 114.03 yen late Thursday from 113.65 yen late Wednesday.

Earlier this year, the dollar advanced to multi-year highs, prompting forecasts that U.S. exports would become uncompetitive overseas. Those fears were borne out to some degree on Wednesday when Japan reported that its trade surplus with the United States nearly doubled in May.
But Marc Chandler, a senior currency analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said that trade does not affect the dollar against the yen as much as it used to.

"The Japanese have restructured their economy and they are becoming less dependent on the U.S. as a market for their exports," he said, noting that Japan is focusing more on markets in Southeast Asia.

U.S. President Bill Clinton, in a White House interview with Japanese television before departing for Denver on Thursday, said he was concerned about Japan's large surplus with the United States but said exchange rates should not be used as a way to correct trade imbalances.

In other trading, the dollar was also pressured after weekly data on jobless claims fuelled bets that the Federal Reserve would not raise interest rates at its next policy-setting meeting on July 1-2.

The Labour Department report showed a jump in the number of Americans filing for unemployment benefits last week, leading analysts to expect a weak April employment number from the department in two weeks.

"Blend that in and that's why we're seeing a little more dollar weakness against sterling and dollar weakness against marks, whereas yen is sort of definitely a trade issue," said David Durrant, senior currency strategist at I.D.E.A. Inc.
The dollar fell to 1.7235 marks from 1.7333 marks and to 1.4380 Swiss francs from 1.4470. The dollar declined to Canadian $1.3878 from C$1.3935.
